teaser.text: Brookfield Infrastructure Partners sells access to essential networks and facilities rather than one consumer product. A dollar comes in when a customer uses, reserves or receives regulated access to those assets, and it goes out through operating costs, maintenance, growth investment, debt, taxes and distributions.

blocks.heading: Where could BIP's shares be in each forecast year?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast points to C$46.39 first and then lower, hinging on projects becoming cash-producing assets, FFO growing per unit and financing remaining manageable. That first weighted price is forecast for October 2027 and implies -7% including dividends. The final weighted price is C$38.76. It implies -11% including dividends in October 2029.

The bear case has 30% probability. The base case has 50%. The bull case has 20%. The investment case strengthens when contracted, powered capacity enters service and reinvested sale proceeds earn attractive returns.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for BIP?

paragraphs.text: The bear case falls to US$7,400 million at the first date and ultimately US$5,000 million. It assumes roughly US$1.2 billion of annual erosion because distributions, buybacks and weak earnings outweigh other equity effects. The bull case rises to US$8,500 million initially and US$8,900 million finally. It requires stronger earnings, project commissioning, recycling and positive currency or ownership effects.

blocks.heading: How much cash does BIP really make?

paragraphs.subsection: 1.2 — How the money flows through the group
paragraphs.text: BIP then deducts maintenance capital to calculate AFFO, or funds available for distribution. AFFO is a closer estimate of recurring cash after preserving existing assets, but it is still not cash that can all be paid out immediately. In 2025, AFFO was $1.964 billion and distributions were $1.743 billion. Growth, debt management and asset sales also shaped where the dollars went.

dividend.opening: BIP’s distributions rise from US$1.90 per unit to US$2.14 in the forecast, within management’s 5%–9% annual target. BIP’s 2025 FFO payout ratio was 66%, leaving a margin between operating earnings and distributions.
dividend.closing: The full BIP memo also examines BIP’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does BIP pay in distributions?

paragraphs.text: Base distributions rise from US$1.90 per unit to US$2.14. That reflects the 6% increase approved for 2026 and sits within the 5%–9% annual target. The bear case reaches only US$1.92 after an initial pause and later 3% increases, because debt, maintenance spending and project risk could force cash preservation. The bull case reaches US$2.31 by applying the full 9% target, which requires strong FFO and cash conversion.

blocks.heading: Is BIP's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: FFO is closer to operating performance, but it is not cash in the bank. Adjusted Funds from Operations, or AFFO, goes further by subtracting maintenance capital: the money needed to keep existing assets safe and productive. BIP’s 2025 FFO payout ratio was 66%, leaving a margin between operating earnings and distributions.

paragraphs.text: Management targets 6%–9% organic growth and 5%–9% annual distribution increases. It targets a 60%–70% FFO payout ratio. Guidance calls for 10% FFO-per-unit growth in 2026. It calls for 12% growth over the next 2–3 years. The annual growth-investment target is US$2,000–3,000 million.

The view would move toward the bear case during 2027–2029 if projects are delayed or underused, AI commitments weaken, margins fall or subsidiary debt refinances at higher cost. Those events would reduce FFO, buybacks and distribution capacity. [scenario M1][scenario M2]

blocks.heading: What is BIP's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Operating-earnings growth slowed in 2025, while net income can swing with asset-sale gains and other accounting items. At C$52.99, the next-12-month P/E is 66.1x. The 4.9% distribution yield sits beside C$41,957 million of market value; distributions exceeded operating earnings per share, and book value per share declined over the period shown. FFO per unit growth is the key test.

blocks.heading: Did BIP keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: BIP has kept one visible promise. Its 2025 annual letter said the board approved a 6% increase for 2026 and described it as the seventeenth consecutive year of increases of at least 5%. The record is encouraging, but investors must still ask whether distributions come from durable operating cash flow rather than asset sales, borrowing or new securities.

blocks.heading: What should we watch in BIP’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The November 6, 2026 results call will show whether projects, FFO and asset-sale proceeds are arriving on schedule. That evidence leads to the most important operating test: whether the backlog becomes productive assets.
